text.p: Christiania Bank og Kreditkasse, Norway's second biggest bank, on Tuesday reported its second best quarterly operating profit before loan losses thanks partly to a sharp rise in income from non-core business.
The first-quarter figure rose 19 percent from the corresponding 1996 period to 592 million crowns ($83.5 million), the best such result since the first quarter of 1993, the bank said in a statement.
Christiania plans to merge with Storebrand, Norway's biggest insurance company, this year to form the biggest financial institution in the country.
The operating profit after losses in the first quarter of 1997 increased 23 percent to 692 million crowns, beating market expectations and sending the share higher on the Oslo Bourse.
The net profit was 685 million million, up 23 percent. This profit corresponds to 1.24 crowns per share, up from 1.01.

Net interest income increased to 884 million crowns from 858 million despite tight interest margins while non-interest income, or non-core business, rose to 511 million from 377 million, an increase of 35 percent.

"The bank's income side shows a positive development, and particularly the activities in Christiania Markets and the bank's funds management area contribute to the increased income," a statement said.
"In addition the Bank has a net income from loan losses for the ninth successive quarter."
Net income from loan losses, or writebacks, amounted to 100 million crowns.

"I am highly pleased about this profit. It is satisfying to see that the conscious efforts made in the bank's capital market activities are yielding results," Borger A. Lenth, outgoing President and Chief Executive Officer, said in the statement.
He will be replaced next month by Tom Ruud, who is expected to be second in command of the merged group under Storebrand CEO Aage Korsvold.

"The bank's profit is a reflection of the great efforts of all employees in an environment where competition remains keen and pressures on interest rate margins have not yet come to a stop," Lenth said.
Net gains on securities rose to 74 million crowns from 38 million, broken down as 40 million on shares and 34 million on certificates and bonds.

At the end of the quarter, the market value of the portfolio of listed shares was 337 million crowns above its book value. The market value of the portfolio of certificates and bonds was 10 million crowns above the book value.
Net gains from foreign exchange and financial derivatives were 124 million crowns, up from 61 million.

"The reason for these comparatively high gains on foreign exchange and derivatives is in particular the good performance in the bank's own trading in the foreign exchange and interest rate markets," the statement said.
Operating expenses in the first quarter were 803 million million crowns, up from 737 million.
The bank's portfolio of total non-performing commitments was reduced by 100 million crowns to 2.8 billion.

Net non-performing commitments, representing the book value of these commitments, amounted to 1.3 billion which is the same figure as at the turn of the year. Net doubtful commitments in the last quarter remained stable at around 1.1 billion.
At the end of March, the group's total assets were 168.7 billion crowns, an increase of 7.1 billion in the last quarter caused by higher lending volumes to customers and credit institutions.
--Rolf Soderlind, Oslo newsroom +47 22 42 50 41
($ = 7.093 Norwegian Crowns)
